title: Given a number N, count how many structurally unique binary search trees can store values 1 through N, without generating them. Explain the dynamic-programming recurrence derived from choosing each root.
shortTitle: Count of Structurally Unique BSTs (How Many Shapes Exist)

s1_definition.profdef: Count of Structurally Unique BSTs returns only the number of distinct BSTs over N values. It follows from the same root-choice argument as generation, but because we only count, we multiply the number of left-subtree shapes by the number of right-subtree shapes for each root and sum over all roots. This is the Catalan-number recurrence, computed bottom up in O(N squared) time with O(N) space, far cheaper than enumerating the trees.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, before benchmarking interest-tier trees, analytics first wants to know how many distinct tree shapes even exist for N tiers, so they can decide whether to enumerate them. We do not build the trees; we just count. For each tier chosen as the root, the number of whole trees is the count of left shapes times the count of right shapes, and we add that across all roots.
s1_definition.oneliner: Count of trees over N equals the sum over each root of left-count times right-count, which is the Catalan recurrence.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Count of Structurally Unique BSTs returns only the number of distinct BSTs over N values. It follows from the same root-choice argument as generation, but because we only count, we multiply the number of left-subtree shapes by the number of right-subtree shapes for each root and sum over all roots. This is the Catalan-number recurrence, computed bottom up in O(N squared) time with O(N) space, far cheaper than enumerating the trees.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, before benchmarking interest-tier trees, analytics first wants to know how many distinct tree shapes even exist for N tiers, so they can decide whether to enumerate them. We do not build the trees; we just count. For each tier chosen as the root, the number of whole trees is the count of left shapes times the count of right shapes, and we add that across all roots.

**One line to remember:** Count of trees over N equals the sum over each root of left-count times right-count, which is the Catalan recurrence.

sections.s2_technical:
Let `count[k]` be the number of unique BSTs that store k values. There is exactly one way to arrange zero values, the empty tree, and one way to arrange a single value, so `count[0] = 1` and `count[1] = 1`. For a tree of k values, choosing the j-th smallest value as the root leaves j minus one values on the left and k minus j values on the right, contributing `count[j-1] * count[k-j]` trees. Summing over all j gives `count[k]`.

In code this is two nested loops: the outer builds counts from two up to N, and the inner sums the products. For example, `for (int root = 1; root <= k; root++) count[k] += count[root - 1] * count[k - root];`. The result `count[N]` is the answer.

A senior-level nuance is that this is the closed-form Catalan number, but the DP recurrence is the clearer derivation and avoids large factorials and overflow surprises if one is careful; for large N the counts grow beyond a 64-bit range, so a production version would use `BigInteger`. Another nuance is that counting is O(N squared), whereas generating is exponential, so when only the count is needed, generation must be avoided.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — Before the National Bank of India analytics team enumerates interest-tier tree shapes, they need the count of shapes for N tiers to judge whether enumeration is even feasible, because the count explodes with N. This is exactly how Count of Structurally Unique BSTs works: it answers the how-many question cheaply.

Problem 2 — Generating all trees just to count them would be exponential and wasteful. This is why we use the dynamic-programming recurrence, computing the count in quadratic time without building a single tree.

The code defines a `BstCountService` exposing `countShapes(n)` returning a `long` (with a note about BigInteger for large N). A `Demo` prints the count for a few values of N and logs them.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: counting for N up to five.

Step 1: Base cases. count of zero values is one, count of one value is one.

Step 2: For two values, roots are 1 and 2. Root 1 gives count of zero on the left times count of one on the right, which is one. Root 2 gives count of one on the left times count of zero on the right, which is one. The sum is two.

Step 3: For three values, summing over roots gives count[0]*count[2] + count[1]*count[1] + count[2]*count[0], which is 1 times 2 plus 1 times 1 plus 2 times 1 equal to five.

Step 4: For four values the recurrence gives fourteen, and for five values it gives forty-two.

Step 5: The sequence one, two, five, fourteen, forty-two is the Catalan numbers, matching the counts of tree shapes.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Count of Structurally Unique BSTs returns just the number of distinct binary search trees over the values one through N, without building any of them. It follows from the same root-choice argument as generation: if I choose the j-th value as the root, there are count of j minus one shapes on the left and count of N minus j shapes on the right, and because the two sides are independent I multiply them, then I sum that product over every possible root. That is the Catalan-number recurrence, and I compute it bottom up in quadratic time with linear space.

The key reason to use this rather than generating and counting is cost: generation is exponential, while this recurrence is O(N squared), so whenever only the count is needed I never build the trees. I also flag that the counts grow past a 64-bit range for larger N, so a production implementation would switch to BigInteger, making that a deliberate decision rather than an overlooked overflow.

At the National Bank of India I used this as a feasibility precheck before enumerating interest-tier lookup-tree shapes, because the number of shapes explodes with the number of tiers and analytics needed to know up front whether full enumeration was even practical. I filled a small dynamic-programming table with the Catalan recurrence and returned the count cheaply. Explaining the multiply-left-by-right-and-sum-over-roots derivation and the overflow caveat is what shows an interviewer that I can separate counting from generation and pick the cheaper tool when that is all that is required.
